title: Herringbone scarf
subtitle: A dense V-shaped weave structure knitted flat in aran-weight yarn.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in herringbone stitch on 5.5 mm needles with aran-weight yarn, finishing at 22 cm wide by 170 cm long. The herringbone stitch slips stitches and knits two together on every row to build a dense diagonal V pattern that lies flat without curling. The fabric is thicker than a standard scarf in the same yarn.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knitted fabric produced by slipping each first stitch knitwise and knitting two together at the end of each knit row, and slipping each first stitch purlwise and purling two together at the end of each purl row. The offset creates interlocking V shapes across the fabric face.
Insert the right needle into a stitch as if to knit, then transfer it to the right needle without working it. This twists the stitch.
A cast-on that forms a neat elastic edge using the tail and working yarn over two fingers simultaneously.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat in
herringbone stitch

on 5.5 mm needles, finishing at 22 cm wide and 170 cm long. The herringbone pattern works by slipping every first stitch and then knitting two together at the end of the row to keep the stitch count stable, building the characteristic interlocking V-shaped diagonals across every row. The fabric is denser and heavier than a stocking-stitch scarf in the same yarn, which makes a shorter piece as warm as a longer plain one.

Flat construction was chosen because herringbone stitch works naturally back and forth: the RS row builds the knit herringbone and the WS row builds the purl herringbone, and together they lock into the V pattern. The finished scarf needs about 380 m (approximately 220 g) of aran-weight yarn. The dense construction means the scarf wraps around the neck once with enough weight to stay in place.
What you need

items.name: Aran-weight wool or wool-blend yarn
items.substitutions: Wool gives the best definition for herringbone. Smooth yarn shows the V pattern more clearly than a fuzzy or bouclé yarn.

items.name: 5.5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 5 / US 9)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular 60 cm or longer
items.substitutions: Go up to 6 mm if your tension runs tight.

content.text: Gauge

17 sts x 22 rows = 10 x 10 cm in herringbone stitch on 5.5 mm needles, blocked. The herringbone fabric compresses the stitch count relative to stocking stitch because the slipped stitches draw the columns together. Swatch at least 8 cm in herringbone and measure after a light block. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge shifts the finished width by about 1.3 cm at this stitch count. Row gauge drift across the full 374 rows changes the finished length by up to 15 cm.
Stitches used
K (knit): right needle from left to right through front of stitch, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through.
P (purl): right needle from right to left through front of stitch with yarn in front, wrap yarn, draw loop through to back.
Sl1 knitwise (slip 1 knitwise)
: insert the right needle into the stitch as if to knit and transfer it to the right needle without working it. The stitch arrives twisted on the right needle.
K2tog: knit two stitches together. Used at the end of each knit row to compensate for the slip.
P2tog: purl two stitches together. Used at the end of each purl row to compensate for the slip.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 38 stitches on the needle. Before beginning, calculate the tail length: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 5.5 mm needles (circumference approximately 17.3 mm) and 38 stitches: (17.3 x 38) / 10 + 15 = 65.7 + 15 = about 81 cm. Leave a tail of at least 81 cm before the slip knot.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on you should have 38 stitches on the needle.
Body
Row 1 (RS): Sl1 knitwise, *Sl1 knitwise, K the slipped stitch and the next stitch together (insert needle through both); repeat from * to the last stitch, K1. (38 sts)

Note: a simpler way to read Row 1 is: slip 1 knitwise, then work across as follows -- slip one knitwise, pass the slipped stitch over the one already on the right needle (this is the herringbone slip), knit one; repeat to end. The stitch count remains 38 because each slip is paired with a knit.
Row 2 (WS): Sl1 purlwise, *Sl1 purlwise, pass the slipped stitch over, P1; repeat from * to end. (38 sts)
Repeat rows 1 and 2 until the scarf measures 170 cm from the cast-on edge. At the halfway mark (approximately row 187, around 85 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 187 you should have 38 stitches on the needle.
Bind off

Work a standard bind-off on a right-side row, knitting each stitch and passing the previous stitch over. Work at relaxed tension as the herringbone fabric can draw in at the cast-off edge if worked tight.
Common faults

Stitch count drifting up. Each row should slip one stitch then pass it over another on every pair, keeping the count stable at 38. If the count rises, a slip was missed and a slip-then-pass step became just a knit. Check the count every 10 rows.

Herringbone pattern showing gaps or holes. This happens when the yarn catches on the slipped stitch instead of sliding cleanly past it. Slow down on the slip and ensure the yarn is held at a consistent tension, neither too tight nor too loose, before working the following knit stitch.
Edges curling slightly. The herringbone fabric is firmer than stocking stitch but can still curl a little on the cast-on and cast-off edges. A light block resolves this; no border is needed.
Finishing

Weave in both tails along the wrong-side edge and trim close. The herringbone fabric benefits from a light wet block to even out the slipped stitches. Soak briefly in cool water, press out gently, and pin to shape while damp.
Care
Handwash in cool water with wool wash. Lay flat to dry. The dense fabric dries more slowly than a lighter stitch pattern.
What to try next

The herringbone stitch is a good gateway to other textured slip-stitch fabrics. From here, try the brioche scarf for a loftier, airier slip-stitch texture, or the fisherman's rib scarf for a deep two-colour ribbed effect using a similar knit-below technique.
